title: Counting the units
hookLine: two at dawn, four, four, three at sunset, four at night

cards: Some things you learn as a rhythm before you learn them as facts. Thirty days has September. A phone number sung in an old commercial.
The daily prayers can be learned the same way, as a string of numbers said in one breath: two, four, four, three, four. It sounds like a code.
It's actually a map of the whole day, and each number counts one thing: a unit of the prayer. You've learned every piece of it this week. Today, how the pieces add up.

teach.b: The unit is called a rak'ah, from the same root as ruku', the bow. One rak'ah is one full cycle: standing and reciting, the bow, rising, two prostrations with the sitting between.
The pieces from this past week, in order, make one rak'ah, and the daily prayers are built out of them. Fajr, at dawn: two. Dhuhr, midday: four.
Asr, afternoon: four. Maghrib, sunset: three. Isha, night: four.

Seventeen in all, every day. After every second rak'ah the person sits for the tashahhud, and in the last one adds the taslim, so a four-rak'ah prayer has a sitting in the middle and one at the end. Why these numbers?
The tradition keeps them because this is how the Prophet ﷺ prayed. But there's a story in them.
Aisha, his wife, said in a hadith in Bukhari that the prayer was first made obligatory as two rak'ahs each.

teach.h: ON THE ROAD, FOUR BECOMES TWO.
teach.b: Then the traveler's prayer was left at two, and the prayer at home was increased. That's why, to this day, a traveler shortens the fours to two.
The Qur'an gives the permission, in Surah an-Nisa: no sin in shortening the prayer on a journey.
The dawn prayer stays two; the sunset prayer stays three. So the numbers carry a little history: two was the original shape, the day's middle prayers grew, and on the road the fours go back to two.

how: Muslims pray seventeen obligatory rak'ahs a day: two at fajr, four at dhuhr, four at asr, three at maghrib and four at isha, and travelers commonly shorten the four-rak'ah prayers to two.

o: one of the five daily prayer times
a unit of time, about an hour long
one full cycle of the prayer's movements

games.q: how many units? tap the pairs.

s: a rak'ah is just the bow
the word comes from ruku', but a rak'ah is a full cycle, standing to the second prostration.
Aisha said the prayers were first two rak'ahs each
then the home prayer was increased and the traveler's left at two (Bukhari).
travelers must pray the full four
the Qur'an says there's no sin in shortening the prayer on a journey.

games.q: you're on a long journey and it's time for dhuhr, normally four rak'ahs. what does the tradition allow?
games.why: a traveler shortens the four-rak'ah prayers to two; Aisha said the traveler's prayer was simply left at the original two.

practice: Hold up your hand and count it through: thumb, fajr, two; index finger, dhuhr, four; middle finger, asr, four; ring finger, maghrib, three; little finger, isha, four.

Then say just the numbers, two, four, four, three, four, let your hand rest, and picture one whole rak'ah, from standing to the second prostration, slowly. If you pray, you'll know where you'll be at the next one.

wordCard.voice: Rak'ah. One unit of prayer, from standing to the second prostration; seventeen of them every day. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: one unit of prayer, from the root of ruku', the bow.

carryVoice: Your line: two, four, four, three, four. Seventeen units, the whole day in one breath. Day one hundred nine, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 350 (Aisha: the prayer first made obligatory as two rak'ahs)
Qur'an 4:101 (no sin in shortening the prayer on a journey)
